response:
It sounds frustrating to have a coping tool that works well most days, only to have it feel unavailable when you need it most. That's actually really common with test anxiety—the pressure of the moment can make it hard to access skills, so it helps to have a few extra strategies.

A few things worth trying: practice a grounding technique like the 5-4-3-2-1 method (naming things you see, hear, touch, etc.) to redirect your mind when breathing alone isn't enough. Preparing under test-like conditions beforehand can also reduce the shock of the real thing. And in the moment, try writing down anxious thoughts for a couple minutes before starting—research suggests this "brain dump" can free up mental space. Reminding yourself that a bit of nervousness is normal, not proof you'll fail, can lower the pressure too.

If this anxiety is significantly affecting your grades or wellbeing, talking with a counselor or your school's support services could help you find more tailored tools.
